title: At work: job satisfaction
subtitle: run-of-the-mill, perks, work-life balance, skeleton staff
summary: Discuss what makes a job worth doing - morale, teamwork, stability and work-life balance - and the perks, entitlements and redundancies that go with working life.

lesson.heading: What is job satisfaction?
lesson.text: **Job satisfaction** is the feeling that your job is worth doing and fulfils you. Is it just having a pleasant **workplace**, the place where you work, or is it more than that? Can a **run-of-the-mill** job - an ordinary one, not special or exciting - be satisfying?

examples.text: Some people put up with a stressful job if it means short-term **financial reward**.
examples.note: financial reward = money gained; the opposite of short-term is long-term

examples.text: I don't think that **financial reward** is the key to **job satisfaction**.
Amy joined the law firm for the **long-term** career prospects they offered.

lesson.heading: Morale, teamwork and stability
lesson.text: **Morale** is the amount of confidence felt by a person or group. **Teamwork** is working together for a common purpose. **Job stability** means that your job is not likely to change - for some people that matters more than an exciting, high-risk career.

examples.text: Staff **morale** has been very low since the company announced a freeze on pay rises.
Our new manager is very keen to encourage **teamwork** to help us solve problems.
Rafael has done the same job for fifteen years and it will be secure until he retires. For Rafael, **job stability** is very important.

lesson.heading: Work-life balance and dynamic industries
lesson.text: Your **work-life balance** is the amount of time spent working compared to the time spent doing things you enjoy. A **fast-moving** industry develops or changes very quickly, and a **dynamic** company is continuously developing. Someone who is **demotivated** feels less enthusiastic about work.

examples.text: Kate has a good **work-life balance**. She never works late and often finds time to relax with her family.
After graduating, Dan started work in the **fast-moving** film industry.
Daniel's job in a **dynamic** new company is often challenging but exciting.
Chloe is **demotivated** in her current job following recent changes in the finance sector.

lesson.heading: Learn these near-synonyms in pairs
lesson.note: We say look to, meaning consider or plan - not look for: I'm looking to join a dynamic team.

lesson.heading: Leave for a new child
lesson.text: In many countries women are allowed **maternity leave** and men **paternity leave** if they are having a baby; together these are **parental leave**. If a couple adopt a child, they may have a right to **adoption leave** - time away from work to prepare for and look after the new child.

examples.text: She was on **maternity leave** for three months after the birth of her baby.
Then her husband took **paternity leave** for three months.
Sarah has been on **adoption leave** since she and Brian welcomed their new child into the family.

lesson.heading: Money and extras
lesson.text: **Perks** (informal) or **extra benefits** (formal) are the things you get apart from your salary, such as a car or health insurance. Your **holiday entitlement** is the number of days you have the right to take as holiday. **Salary increments** are formal yearly increases; **performance-related pay rises** depend on how well you do your job, and an **annual bonus** is extra money paid once a year.

examples.text: I get some good **perks** in my new job. I get a company car and free health insurance.
My **holiday entitlement** is four weeks a year.
Sales staff are often paid an **annual bonus** when they perform well.
Most people think they are **overworked and underpaid**.

lesson.heading: When times are hard
lesson.text: In a recession a company may announce **voluntary** or **compulsory redundancies** - people losing their jobs, either by offering to go or having no choice. A **skeleton staff** is the minimum number of workers needed to keep operating. The **interview panel** is the group of people interviewing someone for a job.

examples.text: There had been a large number of **compulsory redundancies** at the factory.
Brian took **voluntary redundancy** from his job, which means he is at home too.
During the strike, the airport managed to continue running with a **skeleton staff** of volunteers.
The people on the **interview panel** at the last job I applied for were so unfriendly that I got very nervous.

lesson.text: Look to means consider or plan - I'm looking to join a dynamic team. Look for means search for, and is not used that way here.

exercises.prompt: Do you enjoy ___? Our new manager is keen to encourage it so that we solve problems together.
exercises.hint: (working as part of a team, one word)
exercises.explanation: Teamwork is working together for a common purpose.

exercises.prompt: I don't think that ___ reward is the key to job satisfaction.
exercises.explanation: Financial reward means the money you gain from a job.

exercises.prompt: Would you feel nervous giving a presentation to an ___ at your interview?
exercises.hint: (two words: the group who interview you)
exercises.explanation: The interview panel is the group of people interviewing someone for a job.

exercises.prompt: Sales staff are often paid an annual ___ when they perform well.
exercises.explanation: An annual bonus is extra money paid once a year, usually based on good performance.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of a very unusual, exciting job is a ___ job.
exercises.explanation: A run-of-the-mill job is an ordinary one, not special or exciting.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of a person who is highly motivated is a person who is ___.
exercises.explanation: Someone who is demotivated feels less enthusiastic about work.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of a drop in salary is a salary ___.
exercises.explanation: A salary increment is a formal word for a pay increase.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of a full staff of workers is a ___ staff of workers.
exercises.explanation: A skeleton staff is the minimum number of workers needed to keep operating.

exercises.prompt: Rafael has done the same job for fifteen years and it will be secure until he retires. For Rafael, ___ is very important.
exercises.explanation: Job stability means your job is not likely to change.

exercises.prompt: Kate has a good ___. She never works late and often finds time to relax with her family.
exercises.explanation: Your work-life balance compares time spent working with time spent doing what you enjoy.

exercises.prompt: After graduating, Dan started work in the ___ film industry.
exercises.explanation: A fast-moving industry develops or changes very quickly; dynamic is a close synonym.

exercises.prompt: Amy joined the law firm for the ___ career prospects they offered. She could later become a senior partner.
exercises.explanation: Long-term is the opposite of short-term - the reward comes later.

exercises.statement: When I applied for the job, I was looking for join a dynamic team.
exercises.explanation: We say look to, meaning consider or plan: I was looking to join a dynamic team.

exercises.statement: The atmosphere in my place for work is very pleasant.
exercises.explanation: The word is workplace: The atmosphere in my workplace is very pleasant.

exercises.statement: If someone takes voluntary redundancy, they have offered to leave rather than being forced to.
exercises.explanation: Correct - compulsory redundancy is when the worker has no choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its meaning.

pairs.right: extras such as a company car or health insurance
the number of days you may take as holiday
the amount of confidence a group feels
time off work for a mother with a new baby
time off work to look after an adopted child
money that depends on how well you do your job

exercises.prompt: Is each item a good thing for an employee, or a bad one?
Put this humorous fixed expression into a sentence.
exercises.answer: Most people think they are overworked and underpaid
exercises.explanation: Overworked and underpaid is an informal, humorous fixed expression - the two words always come in this order.
